Nous sommes le 3 octobre, il est 18 h. A: It’s October 3, 6 p.m. Anita John is among the first in the group to protest in front of the Villeray–Saint-Michel–Parc-Extension borough hall. In her hand is a sign showing a car, a peace symbol and a bicycle. She takes the megaphone to voice her concern: when she comes home from work, she sometimes spends up to 30 minutes looking for a parking spot. Shouts of support answer her.
Anita vit à Parc-Ex depuis 1998. Elle es: Anita has lived in Parc-Ex since 1998. She is a nurse and sometimes has to work double shifts because of the staff shortage in Quebec’s health sector.
Anita John est infirmière. Lorsqu'elle r: Anita John is a nurse. When she comes home from work, she spends up to 30 minutes looking for a parking spot near her home. Photo: María Gabriela Aguzzi
« Parfois, [les patrons] me demandent si: “Sometimes [my bosses] ask me if I can work later and I do; so I get home at midnight, and by then, there’s no parking spot. I’m scared of what’s going to happen this winter.” The anxiety shows on her face. “When there’s snow, I’ll have to park far away, and I could slip, fall and hurt myself,” she worries.
L’aménagement de pistes cyclables, elle: Yet she supports the bike lanes. She even says she benefits from them: “I like bikes, my granddaughters use them and that’s very important. The problem is they’re taking away our parking spots,” the nurse repeats.
Le débat sur les pistes cyclables de Par: The debate over bike lanes in Parc-Extension began in June, after the borough held an information session on the upcoming work. Five months later, the protests continue: on November 7, residents opposed to the project once again set out to protest and make themselves heard at the very moment the borough council’s monthly meeting was taking place. Their demand? “Restore our parking and prevent any further removal of parking spaces in our borough without public consultation.”
Entre ceux qui réclament, haut et fort,: Between those loudly demanding “We want our parking spots!” and those shouting “We want our bike lanes!”, common ground seems hard to find.
Laurence Lavigne Lalonde, la mairesse de: Laurence Lavigne Lalonde, the mayor of Villeray–Saint-Michel–Parc-Extension, has taken a position in the debate. And work has already begun.
Mais ce débat va au-delà de la mobilité,: But this debate goes beyond mobility, notably because the borough is undergoing rapid change. Many residents fear it is on the road to gentrification, as happened before in the Plateau-Mont-Royal and Rosemont and, more recently, in Verdun and Hochelaga-Maisonneuve.
Parc-Extension est densément peuplé, et: Parc-Extension is densely populated, and 43% of its residents live below the poverty line. It is the neighbourhood with the largest number of immigrants and visible minorities, making up nearly 60% of its residents. They come mainly from Greece, India, Bangladesh and Pakistan. The neighbourhood also welcomes more newcomers than the Montréal average. Among the families with children who live there, 83% are immigrants.
Actuellement, la mairie met en œuvre un: The borough is currently carrying out a project in line with the aspirations of the Projet Montréal administration: making the city greener. The planet demands it and science confirms it. Bike lanes have thus appeared on Ball, de l’Épée and Querbes avenues. The project requires removing on-street parking on one side of the street.
C’est là que le bât blesse : 250 places: That’s where the shoe pinches: 250 parking spaces have already been removed. The protesters made it clear they were not opposed to bike lanes. Rather, they object to the removal of parking spaces on streets where it was already hard to park.
Pour la mairesse Lavigne Lalonde, la séc: For Mayor Lavigne Lalonde, cyclists’ safety is paramount. Asked why citizens weren’t consulted before the project was launched, she stresses the soundness of the decision, which “helps ensure a certain equity in the quality of infrastructure across the territory.”
Selon les statistiques de la Ville, la m: According to City statistics, half of Parc-Extension residents own a car. What solution is offered to them for getting to work, driving their kids to school, going to the market? “One per cent of public space is dedicated to cycling infrastructure. The rest of public space still serves people who use a vehicle to get to work and for other trips,” the elected official explains. “And when we build infrastructure like this, yes, we remove some parking spaces, but there are still parking spaces. It’s just that people generally have to park a little farther away,” she continues.
Gonzalo Lizarralde est professeur à l’Éc: Gonzalo Lizarralde is a professor at the Université de Montréal’s École d’architecture. Asked about the need to make the city greener, he says he understands the importance of cycling. However, he stresses that the practice can’t be separated from the profile of the people who have adopted it. In this case, they are generally young and healthy. Other users who aren’t in the same position are generally left out. “A family where one person works evenings and heads to work at 8 p.m. in winter won’t ride a bike. A mother with three young children can’t take them to school by bike either,” he points out.
Pour engager le dialogue, l’avenue à pri: To open a dialogue, the path to take should go beyond the opposing positions of environmentalists and car advocates, the researcher believes. “A policy can have many side effects, even if it’s good in theory. Not all of its impacts will be positive, even if the city needs to be improved.”
Selon lui, il est nécessaire de travaill: In his view, in-depth work is needed on how green policies are applied on the ground. “It’s very easy to get carried away by ideologies like sustainable development and green culture, or by narratives that are very common, but you also have to weigh them. Authorities have to do that with concrete data. There are already many examples in Montréal of what has happened in terms of gentrification and what needs to be done. These examples need to be documented and, once they’re documented, used for public policy,” he stresses.
Or, les projets engagés destinés à rédui: Yet projects already underway to reduce car use, like the REV (Réseau express vélo) on Saint-Denis, aren’t sufficiently documented, he says. “Two winters have already gone by, and all we know is that a million people use it every year, but we need a lot more data. Who are the millions of people using it? Are they mostly men, or mostly women? What is their socio-economic status? Do they have children? This is data that even pro-cycling agencies don’t present.”
Les aspects culturels doivent aussi être: Cultural aspects must also be taken into account, the expert believes. Indeed, Parc-Extension is a multi-ethnic neighbourhood where not everyone sees the bicycle as a means of transportation.
Il regrette que des décisions aussi cruc: He regrets that decisions so crucial for residents aren’t made on the basis of prior data studies. “I think that in many cases of gentrification, the problem is shifted, but not solved. When a mayor’s office makes unilateral decisions, there’s a bit of that too. If I impose a rule and those who don’t follow it are asked to leave, I no longer see the problem.”
« Ne pas voir le problème », c’est juste: “Not seeing the problem” is exactly what bothers Miguel Ángel Pérez, a resident and the owner of two rental buildings in Parc-Extension. He has lived in the neighbourhood for 40 years and has no intention of leaving.
Lui aussi a participé à l’une des manife: He too took part in one of the protests held in October. The man, in his fifties, is the reserved type. At the protest, he mostly listened to the speeches. He had made a sign that read: “Keep our parking, Mayor, listen.”
Sa question, en ce moment, est la suivan: His question right now is this: how will he attract new tenants? Prospective renters often ask him whether there’s parking near his buildings.
Miguel Ángel Pérez vit à Parc-Ex, où il: Miguel Ángel Pérez lives in Parc-Ex, where he owns two buildings. Photo: María Gabriela Aguzzi
« Je dois être honnête et leur répondre: “I have to be honest and tell them no. So I won’t be able to rent out the available apartments,” he says, worried. “But it also affects me because I live in one of the buildings and my kids come to visit me. They come by car, and even for them, it’s going to be a problem. Especially in winter, when everything is complicated by the snow.”
Pour celui qui dit bien connaître Parc-E: For a man who says he knows Parc-Extension well, the problem won’t stop there, “because we’re going to start invading other streets to be able to park.”
D’autant que, selon lui, la plupart des: All the more so because, according to him, most immigrants in the neighbourhood need a car to get to work. We don’t have official data on this, but he maintains that most of them have to travel long distances for work, which makes it hard to use alternative means of transportation.
Miguel Ángel regrette aussi que les auto: Miguel Ángel also regrets that municipal authorities say it isn’t the City’s responsibility to guarantee parking spaces. Last September, during question period at the Villeray–Saint-Michel–Parc-Extension council, Mayor Laurence Lavigne Lalonde did indeed state the following: “The City is not responsible for finding a parking space for every car on the territory.”
Martin Saintuce, comme Miguel Ángel, est: Martin Saintuce, like Miguel Ángel, is an immigrant. This neighbourhood resident, with tired eyes and impeccable clothes, acknowledges that finding parking in Parc-Ex isn’t easy. But the problem doesn’t concern him, because he rides a bike, even at 70.
Il habite seul depuis 10 ans, sur l’aven: He has lived alone for 10 years on Outremont Avenue. His children have grown up and moved out. We meet him in early November in front of a Tim Hortons, right near the borough hall where the protesters had gathered a month earlier.
Il nous rejoint à vélo, après avoir parc: He joins us by bike, after riding the six blocks between his home and the Tim Hortons. It’s a route the retiree takes almost every day, to run errands or just for a ride. His eyes reddened by the wind, he says he loves his three-coloured bike, which above all helps him stay in shape. He even rides in winter, “as long as they clear the snow from the streets.”
« Les automobilistes n’aiment pas les cy: “Drivers don’t like cyclists, and that’s the problem right there,” he says, laughing, adding that this is the heart of the debate going on in the neighbourhood. “But I need it every day. For exercise, to stay toned,” says Martin, who seems in great shape.
Martin Saintuce a 70 ans. Il utilise son: Martin Saintuce is 70. He uses his bike every day to run errands and get around, but also to keep fit. Photo: María Gabriela Aguzzi
Selon lui, ceux qui ne sont pas d’accord: In his view, those who disagree with the new bike lanes have a selfish vision of public space. “They only think of themselves. (...) Cyclists have the right, like everyone else, to get around the neighbourhood. There’s no priority for one type of citizen,” he says in a more serious tone.
Quant au fait qu’il sera plus difficile: As for the fact that it will be harder for drivers to park near their homes or businesses, he doesn’t hesitate to answer: “Absolutely. That’s true, because parking is already difficult in Parc-Extension. It’s always been difficult in Parc-Extension,” but for Martin, that can’t be “an obstacle that prevents cyclists like him from having access to safe bike lanes.”
Martin reconnaît également que Parc-Exte: Martin also acknowledges that Parc-Extension has been changing rapidly in recent years and has no doubt that this could affect the neighbourhood’s most disadvantaged families, which worries him.
À cet égard, Gonzalo Lizarralde estime q: On this point, Gonzalo Lizarralde believes the bike lanes add to a series of accelerated changes that are displacing part of the neighbourhood’s poor population. The architect notes that Parc-Extension is in the midst of gentrification, particularly since the construction of the Université de Montréal’s MIL campus, which opened in 2019.
« Ces politiques d’aménagement urbain fi: “These urban planning policies end up displacing people who can’t keep up with the pace of change in cities. This process began several years ago in Parc-Extension and, of course, it’s not the bike lanes that will intensify it, but they’re one element that adds to others in the process,” the architect explains.
La pénurie de logements, le difficile ac: The housing shortage, the difficulty of becoming a homeowner – these are the ills that, according to Mayor Lavigne Lalonde, are driving gentrification on the island of Montréal. She believes building bike lanes has nothing to do with gentrification. “And we’re working on that in lots of other ways to make sure, precisely, that we’re able to build housing,” the mayor says.
Paula Negrón-Poblete, professeure à l’Éc: Paula Negrón-Poblete, a professor at UdeM’s École d’urbanisme et d’architecture de paysage, isn’t surprised the debate is still going on today, given the lack of public consultation. Had such a consultation taken place, it probably would have led to a confrontation, the researcher believes, “but it would have been more interesting to make room for reflection, with questions like: ‘What can we do so that people in Parc-Extension use their cars less?’”
« L’espace public appartient à tout le m: “Public space belongs to everyone, and it’s not just where cars park or the bike lanes. Public space is also the sidewalk and the benches on the streets. If we want people to get around differently, we have to make them want to walk in the neighbourhood,” she explains.
Ainsi, la professeure considère que la m: The professor therefore considers that the measure, while good in nature, was poorly executed, for lack of a broader vision of what mobility involves.
« Si les trottoirs sont plus larges ou s: “If the sidewalks are wider or if benches are installed so people can walk and take breaks, especially seniors, the situation changes. If people see that kind of thing, they might tell themselves that they’ve lost their nearby parking spot, but that they’re getting other benefits.”
Compte tenu de l’absence de terrain d’en: Given the lack of common ground and the fact that the project is going ahead, the mayor is asking the neighbourhood’s residents to adapt. “I can understand that, for some people, it’s a big upheaval,” she says.
Pour elle, ces pistes cyclables offrent: For her, these bike lanes offer freedom, a way to break out of the area’s isolation, so that young people can take part in activities that may be happening a bit farther from home. “They’ll be able to do it safely by bike. So we’re responding to a real need, and one that a lot of citizens are asking for, too.”
